title: Tree Construction and Serialization
summary: Rebuilding a unique tree from traversal pairs, and serializing/deserializing it losslessly — which traversal combinations actually contain enough information.

slides.markdown:
Given two traversal outputs of the same tree, can you rebuild the original tree uniquely? The answer depends entirely on **which two** traversals you're given — some pairs contain enough information, others genuinely don't, no matter how cleverly you try to reconstruct.

The same question, viewed from the other direction, is serialization: encoding a tree into a string (or array) that can later rebuild the exact original shape. Both problems hinge on the same insight — inorder traversal is special because it's the only one that reveals a node's position **relative to both subtrees simultaneously**, which is why it pairs well with either preorder or postorder but preorder-and-postorder alone isn't enough.

slides.subTitle: Root from preorder, split boundary from inorder
slides.markdown:
Preorder's first element is always the tree's root. Once you know the root's value, find that same value in the inorder sequence — everything to its left in inorder is the entire left subtree, everything to its right is the entire right subtree (this follows directly from what inorder means: left subtree, then node, then right subtree).

That split tells you exactly how many elements belong to the left subtree, which lets you carve out the corresponding prefix of the *remaining* preorder sequence (after the root) as the left subtree's preorder, and the rest as the right subtree's — then recurse on each piece with its own preorder/inorder pair. Preorder supplies "who's the root," inorder supplies "how big is each side."

slides.sectionTitle: Building a tree from preorder and inorder
slides.subTitle: In O(n) with an index map
slides.markdown:
```python
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    idx_map = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}  # value -> inorder index, O(1) lookup
    self_idx = [0]  # mutable pointer into preorder

    def helper(left, right):
        if left > right:
            return None
        root_val = preorder[self_idx[0]]
        self_idx[0] += 1
        root = Node(root_val)
        mid = idx_map[root_val]
        root.left = helper(left, mid - 1)
        root.right = helper(mid + 1, right)
        return root

    return helper(0, len(inorder) - 1)
```

The `idx_map` is what keeps this O(n) instead of O(n²) — without it, finding the root's position in inorder requires a linear scan per recursive call, degrading the whole algorithm.

slides.subTitle: Same idea, root comes from the end
slides.markdown:
The mirror-image construction: postorder's **last** element is always the root (since postorder visits the node after both its subtrees). Same inorder-split logic applies — find the root's position in inorder to determine left/right subtree sizes — but now you carve the postorder array from the **end** backward, processing the right subtree before the left, since postorder's structure is (left subtree, right subtree, root) and you're consuming it from the root outward.

The algorithmic shape is identical to preorder+inorder, just with recursion order and array-slicing direction flipped to match where the root sits in the sequence.

slides.sectionTitle: Preorder + postorder alone can't reconstruct a unique tree
slides.subTitle: Without null markers
slides.markdown:
Given only preorder and postorder (no inorder), reconstruction is **ambiguous** for trees where a node has exactly one child — there's no way to tell from these two sequences alone whether that single child is the left or right child.

Concrete example: a root with a single child, value 2. Preorder is `[1, 2]` and postorder is `[2, 1]` regardless of whether node 2 is the left or right child of node 1 — both possible trees produce the identical pair of sequences. Inorder breaks this ambiguity precisely because it places the node *between* its children, revealing which side is empty; preorder and postorder both only ever say "node comes before/after its subtrees," never *which* subtree a lone child belongs to. Full binary trees (every node has 0 or 2 children) don't have this ambiguity, so preorder+postorder does uniquely reconstruct those — but that's a special case, not the general rule.

slides.subTitle: Preorder-with-nulls vs level-order-with-nulls
slides.markdown:
The ambiguity from the previous slide is exactly what serialization formats solve by adding **explicit null markers** — once you know exactly where every missing child is, a single traversal (not a pair) is sufficient to reconstruct the tree unambiguously.

**Preorder-with-nulls**: write the node, then recursively serialize left, then right — writing a sentinel (like `"#"`) wherever a child is missing. Deserializing reads the sequence in the same order, consuming one token per recursive call, and stops descending the moment it reads a null marker.

**Level-order-with-nulls**: the same idea applied breadth-first — write each level, including null markers for missing children, until an entire level is all-null. This is the format most people recognize from visual tree representations (like `[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]`), though it's slightly more complex to implement correctly than the preorder version.

slides.sectionTitle: Serializing and deserializing with preorder and null sentinels

slides.subTitle: Size and simplicity trade-offs
slides.markdown:
| | Preorder + nulls | Level-order + nulls |
|---|---|---|
| Output size | proportional to node count (nulls only at leaf boundaries) | can include a large number of trailing nulls to mark level completion, especially for skewed trees |
| Implementation | simple recursive read/write | needs a queue and careful level-completion tracking |
| Human-readability | less intuitive as a flat string | matches how trees are commonly drawn/visualized |

A heavily skewed tree serialized level-order can produce a surprisingly large number of null tokens, since each level needs both a left and right null marker for every real node without a full set of children — preorder's nulls are bounded tightly by the actual node count instead. Pick preorder+nulls by default for compactness and simplicity; level-order+nulls when matching a specific external format (like a common visualization tool's array notation) matters more than either of those.

slides.sectionTitle: Duplicate values breaking naive index-lookup construction
slides.subTitle: Needing position maps, not value maps
slides.markdown:
The `idx_map = {val: i for ...}` trick from the preorder+inorder construction assumes every value is **unique** — if the tree contains duplicate values, a value-to-index map collapses multiple valid positions into one, silently picking the wrong split point.

```python
# BUG: with duplicate values, this map only keeps the LAST occurrence's index,
# discarding earlier occurrences entirely
idx_map = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}
```

With genuine duplicate values, preorder+inorder (or postorder+inorder) reconstruction becomes **ambiguous in general**, not just an implementation bug — multiple distinct trees can produce the identical pair of traversal sequences when values repeat, so no index-map fix alone restores uniqueness. Most interview versions of this problem explicitly state "all values are unique" for exactly this reason; if that guarantee is missing, it's worth surfacing to the interviewer rather than assuming the map-based approach still works.
